abstract: |
 |  The Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) is a popular model for measuring word associations in text corpora (e.g., biases, stereotypes, schemas). WEAT-like measurement models aim to estimate the difference in association between two concepts indexed by keyword lists over a set of word embeddings. I show that they do not consistently estimate this quantity. The underlying metric, mean cosine similarity, cannot discern what all of the keywords have in common: in keyword lists with at least four words, the metric does not guarantee that every sub-list containing at least three words is closest in association to itself. For this to be true, the Euclidean distance between at least one of the word pairs would have to be negative. The metric is geometrically inconsistent in the sense that this is impossible. The degree of inconsistency is partially predictable from the conditioning of the cosine similarity matrix. The inconsistency of mean cosine similarity is explained in comparison to a multidimensionally consistent similarity metric.
 |

\pagebreak

The Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) is a popular method for measuring word associations in large text corpora using word embeddings [@caliskan2017semantics]. WEAT is modeled on the Implicit Association Test (IAT) in social psychology [@greenwald1998measuring]; like the IAT, it is meant to estimate differences in association between concepts encoded in keyword lists. However, WEAT-like measurement models do not consistently estimate this quantity. Given two keyword lists of cardinality $k$ that are subsets of a word vector space ($A, B \subset W$), the similarity metric underlying WEAT---mean cosine similarity (MCS)---is best understood as a certain estimator of the expected *unidimensional* word association: on average, how much does any pair of individual words $\{A_i, B_i\}$ have in common? This is a mathematically and conceptually distinct quantity from *multidimensional* word association: how much do all of the words in $A$ and all of the words in $B$ have in common? This paper explains why these two seemingly similar word association estimands must not be confused.

More specifically, this paper shows that MCS is geometrically inconsistent estimator for the multidimensional word association estimand, and introduces an alternative similarity metric estimator with consistent geometry. Given any keyword list with more than three words, the MCS metric is not guaranteed to determine that all of the sub-lists are closest in association to themselves. This counterintuitive behavior yields measures that contradict one-another when words are added or withheld from the analysis. Consequently, MCS-based measures of word association are highly dependent on the choice of input keywords. I contrast MCS with a multidimensional similarity metric for word associations with close links to canonical correlation analysis (CCA) [@hotelling1936cca]. CCA yields a geometrically consistent metric --- the sum of the squared cosines of the principal angles between the subspaces spanned by the two keyword lists, hereafter the "canonical subspace metric" --- that is considerably more robust to size and membership perturbations of the input keyword lists.

The paper proceeds as follows. In Section 2, I clarify the goals of word association measurement; discuss the family of generalized log-bilinear estimators (i.e. word embedding algorithms) commonly used to estimate word co-occurrence statistics; and explain how WEAT models propose to measure word associations using word embeddings. In Section 3, I outline the additional metric assumptions that are required when the theoretical word association estimand is intrinsically multidimensional. I show that MCS does not satisfy these assumptions, and I demonstrate that CCA can be applied to construct a geometrically consistent metric. In Section 4, I contrast MCS and CCA estimates for the key quantities of interest in multiple WEAT-like models in the applied word embeddings literature; while CCA yields a consistent metric in every case, the geometric inconsistency of MCS arises regardless of the input word embedding model, resulting in measures with consequential sign and magnitude errors. I conclude in Section 5 with a discussion of the theoretical and methodological challenges of constructing word association measures for research in the social sciences.^[In the Appendix, I discuss the general family of WEAT measurement models, including models that incorporate vector centroids; models that employ different arithmetic mean structures over pairs of keyword lists; and models that include additional cosine-valued quantities as covariates. The extended discussion provides a model-based analysis of "frequency bias" in WEAT-like measures and shows why adjustments for marginal frequency detract from the validity of the model family.]


## Background: Why and how to measure word association

Language is a universal feature of social and political behavior. Consequently, many social science theories implicate the words people say, write, sign, hear, read, and see. To understand how social scientists phrase questions about these phenomena, it is critical to first understand the relationship between word meaning, word association metrics, word co-occurrence distributions, empirical word frequencies, and word embedding algorithms. At a high level, the researcher:

1. begins with a theoretical question about **word meaning**, which defines a (potentially infinite) set of locations in text where that word meaning can be observed;
2. constructs a **sample corpus** consisting of texts where the relevant kind of word use is observable;
3. observes the **empirical word frequency** for each word in the sample corpus;
4. constructs **word co-occurrence distributions** for each word according to a function that defines what it means for words to co-occur, potentially using **word embedding algorithms**; and
5. defines a **word association metric** that links their theoretical question to a comparison of the co-occurrence distributions

To begin, the researcher defines a research goal that requires a description of how people talk (write, sign) or an estimate of the causal effect of people talking (writing, signing) on patterns of human interaction. These research goals in turn require a way of precisely defining word association with respect to the situation in which we are observing language use (i.e., the corpus of text on hand). Word association captures the sense in which words are meaningfully related to one-another when language is used in the way it is used in this situation. What is meant by "related" varies between theories of language use. A generic definition shared by many approaches is that words have related meanings if they are used together (CITE Wittgenstein, Firth). Once the researcher has defined the theoretical word association estimand, their task is to construct a word association metric that connects the theoretical quantity of interest to a quantity that can be estimated from data describing language use (i.e. text).

To do this, the researcher must first assign a number to each pair of words in the sample vocabulary so that pairs that are used together more often in the corpus have larger numbers. A systematic way to assign numbers in this fashion is to estimate a word co-occurrence distribution. Word co-occurrence statistics quantify the relative probability of observing each word in the sample vocabulary. A simple plug-in estimator of the relative probability of each word in the vocabulary is the sample marginal word frequency: the number of times it appears in any position in the observed text corpus. Conventionally this quantity is then divided by the number of word positions in the corpus so that it can be interpreted as a probability measure. Given a word frequency distribution, the researcher can then construct a word co-occurrence statistic by defining a context kernel function that divides the corpus into (possibly overlapping) sets of positions that co-occur with one-another. In earlier approaches to semantic analysis it was more common to use a delimited partition such as documents, paragraphs, or sentences to define the kernel function; in more recent applications, it is more common to define co-occurrence with respect to the portion of the sample vocabulary that occurs within a small "context window" of each word appearance. Again, it is common to scale this quantity by the total number of co-occurrences in the corpus (as defined by the context kernel function) so that it has a probabilistic interpretation. Once the researcher has estimated a word co-occurrence distribution, they are in a position to construct a word association metric that compares the word co-occurrence distributions of two sets of words.

This procedure has two particularly challenging aspects, one conceptual and one practical. Conceptually, connecting the word association metric to the original theoretical word association estimand imposes certain logical requirements on the choice of metric, depending on the *dimensionality* implied by the research goal. In the simplest case, a researcher might be interested in a unidimensional association between a single pair of words, for example the association between "cats" and "dogs". This association is unidimensional in the sense that it only provides enough information to distinguish the words in one way. In this example, "cats" and "dogs" are related in the sense that feline and canine animals relate to one-another, but also in the sense that they are both pluralized, and plural words appear in specific kinds of sentences. When the research goal targets the association between larger sets of words, the word association problem also becomes multidimensional, in the sense that it is no longer safe to assume that the targeted association is unidimensional. The multidimensionality of the problem is unavoidable because the number of ways a set can be partitioned is proportional to its cardinality. In this setting, as we add more words to two word lists, the number of distinct ways that the lists can be associated increases. For example, if we target the association between \{"cats", "cat"\} and \{"dogs", "dog"\}, we can now differentiate between the association due to common use in contexts where plural words appear regardless of whether they are feline or canine, and the association between feline and canine words regardless of whether they are pluralized. This paper focuses on the relationship between unidimensional and multidimensional word association problems, and in particular the assumptions required for the metric to be logically consistent as the dimensionality *changes*. I return to this topic in Section 3.


### Word embeddings approximate word co-occurrence distributions

In practice, research in statistical text analysis often requires working with large text corpora and correspondingly large sample vocabularies. Corpus size is the source of many practical problems. In particular, when the sample of text is very large, it can require prohibitively large amounts of time and memory to compute co-occurrence frequency distributions exactly. To deal with this problem, computational social scientists have borrowed two information retrieval techniques designed to enable fast interactions with large text corpora: "word embeddings" and "cosine similarity" [@salton1989automatic]. To clarify how these tools alleviate co-occurrence estimation issues, it is helpful to introduce some formal notation.

A word co-occurrence frequency distribution is defined by a Euclidean inner product space $V \times V \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that takes two words in the sample vocabulary $V$ and outputs a scalar describing how much they are used together. The result of applying this function to every word pair in $V$ is an $n \times n$ co-occurrence matrix ($X$). The entries of $X$ are a function of the co-occurrence frequency of the $\{i, j\}$-th word pair. The term "word embeddings" refers to the output of a family of algorithms that approximate this bilinear map using two matrices of rank $p \ll n$, yielding an "embedding" of the co-occurrence distribution of each word in a space of much lower dimension. Formally, the key outputs of a word embedding algorithm are two $n \times p$ matrices $W_R, W_C$ corresponding to the left and right vector spaces $\mathfrak{W}_R, \mathfrak{W}_C$ of this matrix. Researchers typically use the left row vectors $W(i) \in W_R$ as the word embeddings, i.e., as a representation of the distribution of each word's co-occurrences.^[Pennington et al. (2014) propose using the summed matrix $W=W_R+W_C$ in prediction tasks. While this may be useful for prediction tasks, readers should be aware that it considerably complicates the geometric interpretation of the model. In some applications of this model it may be advantageous to retain $W_C$ separately.]

For the purposes of this paper, the key fact about word embedding algorithms is that they replace the word co-occurrence distribution with a Euclidean inner product space of lower dimension. The rank hyperparameter $p$ is the key input to the model apart from the text corpus. It controls the reconstruction error in the approximation indirectly by setting the dimension of the embedding space. The optimal choice of $p$ is application dependent. In predictive applications, the optimal reconstruction error is rarely zero. Allowing for some bias in the estimator is often helpful for improving the generalizability of the model's predictions to unseen text corpora. 
- words are vectors, not points. vectors are defined *with respect to a fixed point*; this is what gives them *magnitude* and *direction*.

The general word embedding estimator for the co-occurrence frequency of word $i$ and word $j$, $X_{ij}$ is
$$g(X_{ij}) = W_R(i)\cdot W_C(j) + b_R(i) + b_C(j) + \epsilon_{ij}$$  
where $W_R(i), W_C(j)$ are two row vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ and $b_R(i), b_C(j)$ are scalar row space and column space intercepts. This expression captures both the GloVe model (Pennington et al. 2014) and the skip-gram negative sampling model (SGNS or "word2vec"; Mikolov et al. 2013a, b). The two main differences between these estimators are (1) the handling of estimation uncertainty in the unilinear terms $b_R, b_C$ and (2) the choice of link function $g$.

#### Intercept uncertainty.

In GloVe the unilinear terms are treated as random intercepts and are estimated from the data during model fitting. In expectation, the sum of the GloVe random intercept terms for each word is approximately equal to the negative log of its frequency $-\log(N_i)$. In the skip-gram negative sampling model, the unilinear terms are incorporated as a fixed empirical prior on the co-occurrence statistic. This quantity is equal to the orthogonal product of the marginal relative frequencies multiplicatively weighted by a "negative sampling" constant (Levy \& Goldberg 2014); this is asymptotically equivalent to a log-bilinear factor model over the pointwise mutual information matrix (Church and Hanks 1990; Levy \& Goldberg 2014).

#### Link function.

The choice of link function $g$ is more consequential. Models in this family assume that the count data are truncated. ; the logarithmic transformation ensures that the model always predicts a positive value for the co-occurrence statistic $X_ij$. The word2vec link function is $\max(\log(\frac{X_{ij}}{X_iX_j})-c, \min(N(W)))$ where $c$ is either zero or a small constant that does not vary with the data. Note that $c$ can be absorbed into the ratio if we let $c = \log(d)$. This function is sometimes called "positive" pointwise mutual information, but note that this is a misnomer as the quantity is non-negative and not positive per se.
- it's a mixture of three likelihoods: the probability of observing zero, the low-frequency region, and the unweighted co-occurrences.
- The link function assumes that the count matrix $X$ has been truncated at zero.
- GloVe implements a similar link function at estimation time by ignoring word pairs that do not co-occur when constructing $X_{ij}$.  
- In addition to the truncated regression link function, the estimator is typically weighted by a plug-in estimator of the data in the low-frequency region, the model exhibits nonlinear behavior. Because the input vector spaces are anisotropic --- the rows and columns of $X$ do not have constant variance --- researchers have found it useful in practice to weight the estimator by the co-occurrence frequency distribution.
- (A general theme in the word embedding estimation literature is that the vast majority of the error in the model seems to be in the very low-frequency range, so anything that can be done to adjust for this fact helps the prediction quality a lot.)


### Testing word associations in the social sciences

The most widely-used family of measurement models for estimating differences in word association between sets of keywords builds from the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) model developed by Caliskan, Bryson and Narayanan (CITE 2017). WEAT models are defined by three operations on the input word embeddings: a pairwise word association function $f_W: W \times W \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that quantifies the word association between any two words indexed in $W$; a keyword selection function $g(W)$ that identifies the targeted concepts with keyword lists; and a conditional expectation function $\mathbb{E}[f_W|g(W)]$ that estimates the difference in mean pairwise word association across the keyword lists.

#### Pairwise word association function.

The standard quantity for the association between two word vectors $w_a, w_b \in W$ is the ratio of their Euclidean inner product (i.e. their dot product) to the product of their Euclidean norms. This quantity is equivalent to the cosine of the central angle between the two vectors, i.e., the angle formed by their intersection at the origin. For that reason it is commonly called "cosine similarity" in applied research, denoted $\cos(w_a, w_b)$. Since the two vectors are "centered" by construction, this quantity is also equivalent to the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient in the row space of $W$ (CITE Rodgers and Nicewander). This fact reflects the practical reason why cosine similarity is widely used as a semantic comparison metric in information retrieval applications: it quantifies the amount of variation in one word that is linearly predictable by orthogonal projection onto the span of the other word vector.

The utility of cosine similarity as a predictive distributional comparison metric is part of the original motivation for applying word embedding algorithms to social scientific word association measurement. However, it is important to remember that precise, valid measurement and fast, optimal prediction are not the same research goal. The key practical difference is that in information retrieval applications, cosine similarity is not directly used as a quantity of interest. Information retrieval applications pose search problems. In search problems, the researcher is concerned with optimally finding relevant documents, so there is no need to worry about *how* the search is performed as long as it yields a good ranking. We care about what we retrieve, and how we retrieve it is only interesting to the extent that we find good matches. In contrast, the measurement of word associations in the social sciences is more or less pursuing the inverse goal: what we retrieve is only interesting insofar as we can say it is because we have identified an interpretable measure of the form of relatedness we are interested in. Consequently, while cosine similarity is a satisfactory plug-in heuristic for a range of prediction problems, social science applications must also establish a logical correspondence between the theoretical word association estimand and any proposed cosine similarity-based measurement model.^[The term "similarity" is unfortunately semantically evocative; as with lists of keywords, it is important to not assume too much based on the way it is labeled. Throughout the paper I avoid the use of "similarity" to describe the word association quantity $d$. I use the term "metric" only when the quantity is a metric in the strict sense of defining a metric space with respect to the vector space $\mathfrak{W}$.]

#### Keyword selection function.

To specify a WEAT-like model, the researcher selects two pairs of disjoint subsets of the rows of $W$ with labels corresponding to a set of keyword lists of length $k > 1$. Formally, let $A, B; C, D$ be the paired subsets of row vectors in $W$ induced by four mutually disjoint keyword lists of equal length $k < p$; for brevity, I only consider the case of equal word list lengths. Keyword selection is typically performed using fixed lists from the social-psychological literature that represent putatively binary distinctions; the label on each keyword list is the concept that the researcher intends the list to represent. The intent behind selecting multiple words for each concept label is to acquire a more general representation of whatever concepts, traits, attributes, identities (etc.) correspond to the social process of interest. For example, Table XXXX lists the keywords for a WEAT sentiment analysis model in which the researcher is interested in the differential association between "male" or "female" words and "pleasant" or "unpleasant" words.

The main assumption needed to connect the targeted concepts to the pair of keyword lists is that each list unambiguously distinguishes its concept. In other words, we assume that we cannot add irrelevant keywords to the analysis. This assumption is implicit in the non-random selection of keywords after identifying the target concept. Irrelevance is relative: each keyword only has to be more related to the target concept than a word selected uniformly at random from the vocabulary would be. However, this requirement also applies with respect to the other keyword list: we have to be able to say that  This aspect of the assumption is harder to satisfy in practice than it might seem. Researchers almost always have the target concept in mind and then select the keywords non-randomly with respect to that keyword, so equally valid alternative conceptual connections are not always obvious. 
A single keyword list can be ambiguous. The keyword list “he, him, his, himself” is not sufficient for indexing “maleness” because it could also index “pronouns”.
A pair of keyword lists can be ambiguous with respect to one-another. For example, if the concepts are “tea” and “coffee” and we select the keyword lists “tea, leaf, cup, jasmine” and “coffee, bean, mug, arabica”, the majority of the words in each are related to “plantness”.

#### Conditional expectation function.

To measure the association between two concepts, the researcher constructs a $k \times k$ matrix of cosine similarities between the two sets of word vectors and computes its arithmetic grand mean (hereafter MCS score). It is useful to think of the paired keyword lists $A, B; C, D$ as a function that selects off-diagonal blocks from the global cosine similarity matrix $\Theta$. MCS scores are computed by comparing the arithmetic grand mean of each block, and the WEAT measure is the two-way difference in MCS scores:
$$\text{WEAT}(A, B, C, D) = \frac{1}{k^2}\sum_i^k\sum_j^k\Big(\cos(A_i,C_j) - \cos(A_i,D_j) + \cos(B_i,D_h) - \cos(B_i,C_j)\Big)$$  

Figure XXXX depicts the result of the partition selection and score computation steps with respect to the global cosine matrix. Since $\Theta$ is symmetric, it does not matter whether the two-way difference is taken with respect to the rows or the columns first, so $\{A,B\}$ and $\{C,D\}$ are in some sense interchangeable. Continuing with the gender-sentiment analysis example, it is equally correct to say that the WEAT measure targets (a) the difference in (un)pleasantness between maleness and femaleness or (b) the difference in (fe)maleness between pleasantness and unpleasantness.

As a consequence of the symmetry of the test design, when discussing the geometric properties of this model it is sufficient to characterize the behavior of the underlying MCS score $d_\text{MCS; k} = \frac{1}{k^2}\sum_i^k\sum_j^k\cos(X_i, Y_i)$, for any two disjoint and arbitrarily ordered word vector subsets $X, Y \subset W$ of size $k$. Note that the more general family of WEAT-like models treats the MCS score as the outcome variable in a conditional expectation function. If researchers specify conditional expectations that depend on more complex covariance structures beyond the function that selects $A, B; C, D$ (e.g. exogenous covariates) more complex modeling challenges may come up. However, any model in this family fundamentally rests on the validity of the MCS score as a representation of the association between the concepts indexed by the keyword list selection function.

In the original WEAT paper, the total score is computed by taking the mean in one direction and summing in the other direction, so the denominator is $k$ rather than $k^2$. Extensions applying the model in other contexts more commonly use the arithmetic grand mean, or some other arithmetic structure over $g(W)$. I focus on the behavior of the *sum* as $k$ changes. The sum is the only part of the model that incorporates information from the data; $k$ is entirely dependent on the researcher's choice of a number of keywords. The critical question is whether the sum operation is valid with respect to the choice of word association quantity, and the choice of scaling constant is relatively unimportant.

Consequently, the crucial measurement problem is whether the MCS score (i.e. the sum of cosines) is a valid generalization of the predictability-based word association quantity to multidimensional word association problems. The idea behind looking at many pairwise associations across the input keyword lists is that "[m]any if not most words have multiple meanings, which makes pairwise measurements "noisy". To control for this, we use small baskets of terms to represent a concept" (CITE CBN 2017). In other words, the researcher's intent in constructing keyword lists when applying WEAT-like models is to "average out" the irrelevant meanings of each word so that the estimated quantity reflects the association between the conceptual commonality of all of the words in one list with the conceptual commonality of all the words in the other list. The logic of this research design and its relationship to the underlying word association problem is the subject of the next section.


## Geometric consistency in multidimensional word association measurement

Multidimensional word association problems introduce added complexity to the task of connecting word association metrics. A multidimensional word association problem is posed by any research question that implies a comparison between sets of words of cardinality $k > 1$, where $k$ is chosen by the researcher. In this setting the researcher cannot safely assume that the targeted association is unidimensional. As discussed above, this is essentially the motivation for defining the targeted word association between sets of words rather than between a single pair in the first place. The researcher typically hopes that their analysis is not too sensitive to the choice of number of words: researchers correctly intuit that fixing $k = 1$ would result in an unacceptably non-robust metric. The researcher also hopes the analysis is not too sensitive to the inclusion of any particular word in the analysis. So, a general principle is that a good word association metric is one that does not depend too much in an interpretive sense on the cardinality or composition of the keyword lists. In practice, we can be more precise about this if we are willing to say that "does not depend too much" means something specific about the mathematical behavior of the metric: it must change monotonically with respect to changes in the keyword lists. This requirement breaks down into two linked parts.

First, the metric must be nondecreasing in the composition of each word list as we move them toward one-another. This is equivalent to saying that whatever metric we choose must capture the implicit structure of word associations that is internal to each word list. A good way of understanding this is to imagine that we begin with two identical word lists and are slowly changing one of the word lists into a different list by swapping in different words. For example, imagine that we have two copies of the keyword list "juice, pie, salad, cocktail, cake", and we iteratively change the second keyword list so that it becomes "cherry, apple, lemon, orange, raspberry" one word at a time. Trivially, a good metric is maximized when the two keyword lists are identical. So as we transform the second list, the metric must decrease as the lists differ in more words, because the metric must not imply that swapping in new words would be a better representation of the original list. Note that word replacement is a symmetric operation, since there is a unique way to invert it.

Second, the metric must be nonincreasing with respect to *decreasing* the cardinality $k$ of each word list. Deleting relevant words from the list should monotonically decrease our certainty about the relevant set of commonalities. Removing a redundant word should make very little difference, while removing the more related words should make us less certain For example, imagine we have two word lists "juice, pie, salad, cocktail, cake" and "cherry, apple, lemon, orange, _____", and suppose a seemingly irrelevant word (e.g. "somehow" or "heteroskedastic") is added as the fifth word to the latter list. We would still agree that the main commonality between the words in the list with respect to the other list is "fruit"; the only sense in which adding a completely irrelevant word should change the metric is that if we had instead added some more relevant word (e.g. "raspberry") we would want that addition to increase the metric. This requirement reflects a surprising fact about keyword lists: including and deleting words are not symmetric operations! Given any keyword list, we could in principle include any new word, but we can only remove the words that are already there, so word inclusion and deletion do not invert one-another. This fundamental asymmetry affects how we interpret the consistency of word association quantities. Assuming a fixed list of concept-relevant words, if we include an arbitrary word, whatever quantity we use can change in either direction as $k$ increases. However, again working with a fixed list of words, removing one of the words cannot increase the quantity, unless we are removing a word that we already know is irrelevant.

These two requirements can be combined formally in a general way. In the unidimensional setting, a well-known requirement for defining metrics that are monotonic in composition is the *minimality axiom*, which states that any object $x$ is most similar to itself [@tversky1977features]:  
$$\forall x, y \in W: d(x, y) \geq d(x, x) = 0$$  
However, not all word lists of equal size are uniformly *internally* associated with themselves. In the list "juice, pie, salad, cocktail, cake" the sublist "pie, cake" is more closely related to itself than "pie, salad". So, the zero-equivalence statement $d(x, x) = 0$ applies only when $k = 1$, while a multidimensional word association metric should allow $d(x, x)$ to equal any scalar as long as this is the greatest value of the metric over all of the possible comparisons to $x$. This implies a multidimensional generalization of the minimality axiom:
$$\forall X, Y \subset W: (d(X, Y) - d(X, X)) \geq (d(X, X) - d(X, X)) = 0$$  
This statement holds trivially if $d(X, X) = 0$ as in the original statement of the axiom. Members of the expanded family of quantities that satisfy this requirement in addition to the usual metric axioms are called partial metrics (CITE Matthews).

To incorporate monotonicity in decreasing cardinality, we can assert that the inequality $d(x, y) \geq d(x, x)$ must hold regardless of $k$. Since we can choose any positive $k$ up to the rank of the matrix of co-occurrence statistics (i.e. $p$ if we are approximating it using word embeddings), we need only consider the behavior of the metric as $k$ decreases. Thus we need only assert that partial metric minimality must apply recursively to every $[1,k-1]$-dimensional comparison contained in any $k$-dimensional comparison. Define a multidimensional word association metric as *geometrically consistent* if every $q$-subset of any $k$-subset of the word vectors $W$ is more similar to itself than any other $q$-subset of the same $k$-subset $(k > q)$. Formally, where $[W]^{kCq}$ denotes the set of $q$-subsets of some $k$-subset of $W$, then the following statement must hold:  
$$\forall i, \forall q \text{ s.t. } q < k: \arg\sup_{j} d([W]^{kCq}_i, [W]^{kCq}_j) = i$$  
Intuitively, if the researcher chooses any set of keywords, then every subset they can make by removing one or more words from the set must be more similar to itself with respect to their proposed word association metric than any of the other subsets with the same number of words.

The geometric consistency property is a baseline admissibility criterion for any proposed multidimensional word association metric. A proposed metric without this property is inadmissible because it is self-contradicting as the keyword lists vary in cardinality and composition. Specifically, if some values of $d_{q}(W_X, W_Y)$ are not nondecreasing in $q$, then it cannot be geometrically consistent with respect to $W$. Define the index of inconsistency $\mathcal{I}_{q,k}(d_W(\cdot, \cdot))$ for a similarity metric over $W$ as the proportion of $q$-subsets of a keyword list of cardinality $k$ in $W$ that are most similar to themselves with respect to $d_W(\cdot, \cdot)$. A geometrically consistent metric satisfies $\mathcal{I}_{q,k}(d_W(\cdot, \cdot)) = 1$ for any choice of $q$ and $k$ up to the ambient dimensionality $p$ defined by the choice of $W$. It is particularly worrisome if the expected value of $\mathcal{I}_{q,k}$ is decreasing as $k$ increases, because adding more relevant keywords to an analysis should not make it less consistent as previously discussed. The index of inconsistency is closely related to the regularity of the $k$-simplex induced by $X$; the more regular the simplex is, the more likely it is that  A helpful heuristic discrepancy measure is the Euclidean condition number of $X$, which measures the elongation of its hyperelliptical projection [@golub2013matrix, p.88].

- the metric $d_{q}(W_X, W_Y)$ between the subspaces corresponding to every $q$-subset in $\text{Pow}(X), \text{Pow}(Y)$, where $q \in [1, k_z-1]$. As we increase $k$ to the ambient dimensionality of $W$, the intersection of the orthogonal complements of $W_X$ and $W_Y$ eventually vanishes; that is, regardless of the choice of words, the two subspaces will approach one-another until they coincide exactly once we hit the number of dimensions in the vector space. If $d_{q}(W_X, W_Y)$ is geometrically consistent with respect to $W$, then this must also be true everywhere on the lattice of similarity metrics defined by $\text{Pow}(X), \text{Pow}(Y)$ as $q$ increases to $k$. Thus $d_{q}(W_X, W_Y)$ must be nondecreasing as we increase $q$.


### A consistent metric space for multidimensional word association

To construct a geometrically consistent metric quantity for multidimensional word association problems, let us return to the original definition of the problem. We previously learned that cosine similarity quantifies the linear predictability of one word vector from another word vector. To generalize this quantity to multidimensional problems in a geometrically consistent way, we need a quantity that measures how well one set of word vectors linearly predicts another set of word vectors. This implies that we are interested in a quantity that compares orthogonal projections onto rank $k$ subspaces of $W$.

Define $\mathcal{R}_W(A_k)$ as the row subspace spanned by any $k$-subset $A_k$ of $W$, and denote the orthogonal projection matrix onto $\mathcal{R}_W(A_k)$ as $\mathcal{P}(A_k) = A_k(A_k^TA_k)^{-1}A_k^T$. Formally, if $\mathcal{P}(X), \mathcal{P}(Y)$ are the projection matrices onto two $k$ subsets $X, Y$, we are interested in the linear prediction $\hat{\mathcal{P}}(Y) = \mathcal{P}(X)\mathcal{P}(Y)$. Note that in general, the predicted value $\hat{\mathcal{P}}(Y)$ is not a projection, because projections do not form a group under matrix multiplication. $\hat{\mathcal{P}}(Y)$ is only a projection when we can predict $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ exactly from $\mathcal{P}(X)$; this condition holds whenever $|X|, |Y| \geq p$ (i.e. any $p$ vectors form a basis for $W$). The predicted matrix is equivalent to a group representation by the singular value decomposition theorem $\hat{H}_Y = H_xH_y = USV^T$; we can use this group representation to construct the desired metric. In particular, the matrices $U$ and $V$ define orthogonal rotations of the vector space $W$ such that the rotation $R = UV^T$ satisfies $\mathcal{R}_W(RY) = \mathcal{R}_W(X)$, or vice-versa if the inverse rotation $R^T = VU^T$ is used. Intuitively, $R$ is the *smallest* (i.e. most direct) orthogonal rotation that aligns the common subspace of $X$ with $Y$. (The *result* of this action is invariant to intermediate rotations, since we could always first rotate $W$ into some arbitrary intermediate position defined by orthogonal rotations $Q_1, Q_2$ with respect to U and V respectively, yielding $UQ_1Q_2V^T$; however, the distance traveled is not invariant to the extra rotation.)

The diagonal singular value matrix $S$ defines an inner product on the group of orthogonal rotations in $R^k$ ($S$ is Hermitian and positive semi-definite). $\text{Tr}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(Y))$ describes the amount of dimensionality in which the orthogonal projections onto $\mathcal{R}_W(X)$ and $\mathcal{R}_W(Y)$ coincide. This quantity is very closely related to linear canonical correlation analysis (CCA; CITE hotelling). CCA finds a pair of orthonormal bases for $A$ and $B$ that are minimally angularly separated. By construction, the $i$-th basis vector for $A$ is orthogonal to every basis vector in $B$ except its counterpart. The linear CCA estimator is the Frobenius inner product of the orthogonal projections on the set of orthogonal projections onto rank $k$ subspaces of $\mathcal{R}(W)$ [@krzanowski1979between; @meyer2000matrix, p. 429--430; @borg2005modern, p. 439--441; @horn2012matrix, p. 321]:
$$
\begin{aligned}
d_\text{CCA; k}(W_a, W_b) &= \left<\mathcal{P}(W_a),\mathcal{P}(W_b)\right>_F = \text{tr}(\mathcal{P}(W_a)\mathcal{P}(W_b)).
\end{aligned}
$$  

In $k$ dimensions, if we divide this quantity by the geometric mean of the keyword list cardinalities (i.e. $\sqrt{d^\text{CCA}_k(W_a, W_a)d^\text{CCA}_k(W_b, W_b)}$) (i.e. $k$ if the two keyword lists are equal length) so that it is bounded between 0 and 1, it is the expected dimension of the approximation with respect to the uniform measure on the $n$-sphere (CITE?), or somewhat more intuitively, the amount of variation in $\mathcal{R}(X)$ that is preserved under approximation by $\mathcal{R}(Y)$ (or vice-versa). This quantity has been discussed in many areas of multivariate analysis; in psychometrics it is called Tucker's congruence coefficient [@tucker1951method; @korth1975distribution], and in the French school of data analysis it is more often called the RV coefficient [@escoufier1973traitement; @robert1976unifying].^[Kornblith and colleagues [@kornblith2019similarity] propose using a kernelized version of this quantity to measure similarity between neural network layers. This measure could be used if researchers were using word lists with cardinality larger than $\text{rank}(W)$. In practice, this is not necessary for word association problems of the scale targeted by WEAT-like models.] Since the word embedding literature prefers to think of word vectors as *row* vectors (more on this in a moment) I refer to this expectation as the *canonical subspace metric* to avoid ambiguity. The vector of singular values obtained from the projection matrix product is also substantively interesting; I refer to these component quantities as the *canonical congruences*.

There are two critical modifications to the standard CCA setup involved in computing the canonical subspace metric. First, the analysis is carried out without recentering the vectors that define the canonical subspaces. We avoid recentering because $W$ has a fixed point at the origin, so the angle between any two word vectors (or linear combinations of word vectors) is not invariant to affine transformations. In particular, if we subtract the local centroids from two different subsets of $W$, the overall difference in frequency of use between the two keyword lists distorts the resulting metric.^[This can also be motivated from the perspective of the sparse high-dimensional word association measure approximated by the word embedding matrix. The word vectors lie on the surface of a high-dimensional convex body in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that we have mapped onto a hyperelliptical cross-section in $\mathbb{R}^k$; this surface captures most of the variation in position in the larger space [@dvoretzky1961convex]. However, we must not forget that we are ignoring the remaining $n-k$ dimensions. So, we should think of the word embedding matrix $W$ as missing $n-k$ columns of zeroes. It is safe to omit these columns when we take the unidimensional cosine because this does not affect the calculation of the angular metric once we have constructed the low-rank approximation. But the validity of this angle depends on maintaining the inner product space in which we have approximated the larger space. If we recenter subspaces of $W$ without accounting for the remaining dimensions, the estimated centroids will be very far away from the value we should have used, which is generally quite close to the zero vector due to the large number of dimensions projected into the origin.] Second, as noted above, we carry out the analysis between row subspaces of the same vector space, rather than between the column spaces of two matrices with rows corresponding to the same units. Rather than studying two sets of measures on the same set of observations, we are studying two different sets of observations with respect to the same set of measures, i.e. the variation we have estimated by the word embedding algorithm. The difference is more conventional than substantive. Because the underlying word co-occurrence matrix is symmetric, it is equally valid to view the dimensionality reduction due to the word embedding algorithm as a reduction in the number of *observations* with respect to a fixed number of *variables*.

More importantly, the canonical subspace metric has the desired geometric consistency property. Because the squared cosine of any angle is bounded between 0 and 1 and the canonical congruences lie in mutually orthogonal subspaces, $d^\text{CCA}_k(A, B)$ is constrained to lie between 0, indicating the subspaces share no common direction, and $k=\min(\text{rank}(A), \text{rank}(B))$, indicating the subspaces are exactly aligned in $k$ dimensions. So $d^\text{CCA}_k(A, B)$ is nondecreasing under the action of adding one more vector each to $A$ and $B$. The alignments of the new vectors (1) with respect to one-another and (2) with respect to the existing sets of word vectors completely determine how much the metric grows. If the two new vectors are selected to be the same vector that is orthogonal to both $\mathcal{R}(A)$ and $\mathcal{R}(B)$, then $d^\text{CCA}_k(A, B)$ increases by 1. If the two vectors are orthogonal to one-another and lie completely inside $\mathcal{R}(A), \mathcal{R}(B)$ then $d^\text{CCA}_k(A, B)$ does not change.

$d^\text{CCA}_k(A, B)$ provides a general way of interpreting the usual unidimensional cosine similarity. When $k = 1$, the only nonzero singular value of $\mathcal{P}(A)\mathcal{P}(B)$ is exactly the cosine similarity between the two vectors, so $d_\text{CCA; 1}(W_a, W_b)$ is just $cos^2(W_a, W_b)$. This can be shown by expressing the trace in terms of the Euclidean inner product and norms of the two vectors:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{tr}(\mathcal{P}(w_a)\mathcal{P}(w_b)) &= \text{tr}(w_a(w_a^Tw_a)^{-1}w_a^Tw_b(w_b^Tw_b)^{-1}w_b^T) \\
&= \text{tr}(\frac{1}{||w_a||^2_2||w_b||^2_2} w_aw_a^Tw_bw_b^T) \\
&= \frac{1}{||w_a||^2_2||w_b||^2_2} \text{tr}(w_aw_a^Tw_bw_b^T) \\
&= \frac{w_a^Tw_b}{||w_a||^2_2||w_b||^2_2} \text{tr}(w_aw_b^T) \\
&= \frac{w_a^Tw_bw_a^Tw_b}{||w_a||^2_2||w_b||^2_2} \\
&= \frac{(w_a^Tw_b)^2}{||w_a||^2_2||w_b||^2_2} \\
&= \cos^2(w_a, w_b). \\
&= d^2_\text{MCS,1}(A, B).
\end{aligned}
$$
Consequently, the $k = 1$ case is special in the sense that the MCS score is equivalent to a nonlinear transformation of the general word association metric. But this is not generally true when $k > 1$. This creates considerable inconvenience for MCS-based measurement models.


### MCS is not a geometrically consistent choice of word association metric

We are now in a better position to understand the shortcomings of measurement models based on MCS scores. First consider a word association problem where one of the keyword lists contains only one word. In this limiting case, CCA reduces to multiple linear regression, and the canonical  The arithmetic mean cosine similarity of the single word with all of the words in the larger list can be viewed as a biased estimator of the coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of this model. Consider the vector space $\Theta_w$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$ formed by the cosine similarity between any word vector $w \in W$ and a set of word vectors $X$ with cardinality $k$. Let $\Theta_w(x)$ be the entry for word vector $x$. Denote the $k \times k$ inverse cosine similarity matrix of all pairs of vectors in $X$ as $S_{XX}$. By definition, $S_{XX}$ is positive definite, so we can write $R^2$ as an inner product over $\Theta_w$:  
$$R^2(w) = \Theta^T_w S_{XX} \Theta_w = \left<\Theta_w, \Theta_w\right>_{S_{XX}}$$  

What is necessary for the MCS estimator to be an unbiased estimator for one-to-many word association? As previously noted, to establish this we will not worry about the choice of scaling constant on the mean. We also will not be too concerned with the "squared" part of the coefficient of determination. Concretely, we will ignore the scaling constant $1/k$ and use the mean *squared* cosine similarity as the MCS estimator. This improves the comparability of the estimator with respect to the range of $R^2$ without changing its properties very much. If the estimator were only biased by a known multiplicative constant or monotonic functional transformation, then we could determine which data-independent adjustments we would need apply to get an unbiased estimator. The more fundamental problem is the linear operator $S_{XX}$. The amount of variation in $w$ that can be predicted in the span of $X$ depends on the correlation structure internal to $X$. If we express the bias in the one-to-many MCS estimator with respect to $R^2$, it becomes clear that MCS is unbiased up to a monotonic transformation only when $S_{XX}$ is the identity matrix:  
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Bias}(d^\text{MCS}(w, X)) &=\sum_{x \in X}\big(\Theta_w(x)\big)^2 - \Theta_w S_{XX}\Theta_w(x) \\
&= \sum_{x \in X}\Big(\frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2}\Big)^2 - \sum_{x \in X} \Theta_w(x)S_{XX} \Theta_w(x) \\
&= \sum_{x \in X}\Big(\frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2}\Big)^2 - \sum_{x \in X} \frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2} \cdot S_{XX} \cdot \frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2} \\
&= \sum_{x \in X}\Big(\frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2} \frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2}\Big) - \sum_{x \in X}\Big(\frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2} S_{XX}  \frac{w \cdot x}{||w||_2||x||_2}\Big)
\end{aligned}
$$  
Consequently, the MCS quantity is valid only under a very restrictive assumption about $X$: the vectors in $X$ must be completely orthogonal to one-another.

Finally, to generalize this setup to the many-to-many word association problem setting, consider the cross-cosine matrices $\Theta_{Y|X}, \Theta_{X|Y}$ (note $\Theta_{X|Y} = \Theta^T_{Y|X}$) and the inverse cosine matrices $S_{YY}, S_{XX}$. The diagonal entries of the matrix products $\Theta^T_{Y|X} S_{XX} \Theta_{Y|X}$ and $\Theta^T_{X|Y} S_{YY} \Theta_{X|Y}$ are equivalent to the multiple $R^2$ estimates for all of the one-to-many comparisons from (respectively) $y \in Y$ to $X$ and $x \in X$ to $Y$. Analogously, the off-diagonal entries are the cosine similarities between (say) each vector $y_i$ and the projection of $y_j$ onto the span of $X$.

The canonical congruences are the singular values of $S^{1/2}_{YY} \Theta_{X|Y} S_{XX} \Theta_{Y|X} S^{1/2}_{YY}$ and the canonical subspace metric is $\text{tr}(S^{1/2}_{YY} \Theta_{X|Y} S_{XX} \Theta_{Y|X} S^{1/2}_{YY})$.

This provides a closed form expression for the bias of MCS estimators for many-to-many word association problems:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Bias}(d^\text{MCS}(w, X)) &=\sum_{x \in X}\big(\Theta_w(x)\big)^2 -  \text{tr}(S^{1/2}_{YY} \Theta_{X|Y} S^{1/2}_{XX} S^{1/2}_{XX} \Theta_{Y|X} S^{1/2}_{YY})
\end{aligned}
$$

MCS is biased away from the geometrically consistent quantity in proportion to the pairwise distances among the two inverse cosine matrices and the identity matrix. The geodesic distance between $S_{YY}$ and $S_{XX}$ is equal to $||\text{Log}(S^{-1}_{YY}S_{XX})||_F$ and the geodesic distance from the identity matrix is $||\text{Log}(S_{XX})||_F$, where $\text{Log}(M)$ denotes the matrix logarithm of M (CITE Lang 1999 differential geometry p. 321; Moakher and Batchelor 2005).

we consider the *area* enclosed by the geodesics between the two inverse cosine matrices and the identity matrix with respect to the Lie group of PSD matrices closed under the logarithmic product (CITE Arsigny et al. 2009 SIAM).


This helps to clarify why MCS estimators are fundamentally dependent on the particular choice of keyword list. The entries of the cosine matrix are preserved if vectors are added or removed from $X$ except for the entries directly computed from that vector. This makes it somewhat surprising that the relationship between the MCS score and the canonical subspace metric is so dependent on the choice of keywords. However, the *inverse* of the cosine matrix does not have this property; if we add or remove a vector from $X$, the entries of $S_{XX}$ change (CITE Raveh 1985 inverse correlation). Consequently, if we are running an MCS-type analysis and we examine the cosine matrix under keyword additions or deletions, we will not observe the relevant changes to the correlation structure.



#### MCS is geometrically inconsistent for multidimensional word association problems.

To see the inconsistency concretely, consider the $k$-simplex with edges corresponding to the pairwise Euclidean differences between a set of vectors indexed by any keyword list $X$. This $k$-simplex is bounded by a lattice of $q$-simplical subspaces formed by subsets of $X$ ($q \in [1, k-1], q \in \mathbb{Z}$). An admissible similarity metric must satisfy the minimality inequality with respect to all of the $q$-simplices of equal dimensionality. 

consider the tetrahedron formed by $X=\{\text{he, him, his, himself}\}$. $X$ has triangular faces $X_A = \{\text{he, him, himself}\}$ and $X_B = \{\text{he, him, his}\}$. $X_A$ and $X_B$ coincide at the edge between $\{\text{he, him}\}$, so the dihedral angle between $A$ and $B$ is proportional to the pointwise distance between $\{\text{his}\}$ and $\{\text{himself}\}$. Now consider a proposed metric $d_W^*(\cdot, \cdot)$ that yields the result $d_W^*(X_A, X_A) < d_W^*(X_A, X_B)$. This implies that the distance between $\{\text{himself}\}$ and $\{\text{his}\}$ must be less than zero. $d_W^*(\cdot, \cdot)$ is inadmissible because this is not possible.

In general it is not non-negative for all word pairs $i, j$, and for any three words $i, j, k$ it does not satisfy the triangle inequality $\cos(w_i, w_j) \leq \cos(w_i, w_k) + \cos(w_j, w_k)$. A formal way to say this is to say that the $\{\mathfrak{W}, \cos\}$ is not a metric space.




- For our purposes, the most important consequence of this fact is that the usual family of means does not apply to $\{\mathfrak{W}, \cos\}$! The Frechet mean for a metric space $\{\mathfrak{X}, d\}$ is the set of vectors in $\mathfrak{X}$ that minimizes the sum of the squared metric $d$ with respect to every $x \in \mathfrak{X}$. All of the familiar means (arithmetic, geometric, etc.) are Frechet means with respect to a metric. Unfortunately, if the "metric" we have selected is $\cos(w_i, w_j)$, then none of these means correspond to the expected association of pairs of vectors in $W$ unless we are willing to restrict our attention to a certain subset of $W$.

- If that condition holds, then the underlying set of angles can be interpreted as central angle parameters for the subgroup of orthogonal rotations that move the fixed vector onto the spans of the vectors in the other list [@moakher2002means]. ## Impact on word embedding applications: Two examples

The geometric inconsistency of the MCS model substantially affects the validity of any application of the model. I show this by replicating a suite of WEAT tests for implicit bias in a wide range of word embeddings.

### Setup

#### Word embedding estimation.

I estimate GloVe and SGNS embeddings of all English language articles on Wikipedia as of 1 September 2023. To enhance the comparability of the results, I use only the $W$ matrix from GloVe in lieu of the additive $W+C$ matrix. In the appendix, I reproduce the results in two alternative publicly available word embedding matrices that are widely used in applied settings: the Stanford NLP GloVe embeddings of Wikipedia 2014 and Gigaword 5 text [@pennington2014glove], and the skip-gram negative sampling (i.e. word2vec) embeddings of Google News text [@mikolov2013distributed]. Figures S1-S3 rerun the figures in the paper with the word2vec embeddings; Figures S4-S6 rerun the figures with the Stanford NLP GloVe embeddings. Note that the substantive meaning of the cosine similarity metric differs somewhat between the two spaces because the GloVe embeddings use the $W+C$ representation and the word2vec embeddings use only the $W$ matrix.

#### Canonical subspace metric computation.

I compute the vector of canonical congruences for two sets of row vectors $A, B$ by computing the corresponding orthogonal projection matrices, matrix multiplying them, and taking the singular value decomposition of the resulting matrix. The squared Euclidean norm of the vector of singular values is the canonical subspace metric. In practice, if the canonical congruences are not of direct interest for the analysis (i.e. we only want to quantify the total amount of commonality), then it is not necessary to compute the singular value decomposition. Instead, it is faster to sum all of the values in the matrix obtained by computing the Hadamard (entrywise) product of the two projection matrices. The canonical subspace metric can also be computed in \texttt{R} using the built-in linear CCA function \texttt{cancor} without recentering.

#### Word embedding association tests.

The original paper contains ten example WEAT keyword list sets. A full list of the keywords is provided in the appendix. To ensure the word embedding vocabularies support each analysis, I manually adjust the spelling of some of the words in the original paper. A summary of these adjustments in each set of embeddings is also provided in the appendix. The spelling adjustments are particularly important for the list of Black names derived from the IAT [@greenwald1998measuring], because many of the names in this word list appear to be misspellings and/or close mispronunciations of Black names that are more common in the US context. For example, the list includes the Arabic given name "عائشة"; this is spelled "Aiesha" in the original keyword list, but a far more common spelling of this name in US English is "Aisha"; the word "aisha" appears 2830 times in the corpus, and "aiesha" appears fewer than 50 times. The spelling changes mainly improve the coverage of WEAT 3; in the appendix, I report results for the original spellings.

To illustrate the generality of the MCS inconsistency problem, I also incorporate keyword lists from a number of additional studies in the applied literature that estimate a conditional MCS measurement model.


#### Randomized prediction intervals.

To provide some information about the scale of the canonical congruences relative to our uncertainty about the composition of the input keyword lists, I compare them to the 95% prediction interval obtained by completely randomizing one or both lists. There are parametric significance tests for dependent correlation and congruence coefficients based on the Fisher $Z$-transformation [@korth1975distribution, @steiger1980tests, @bedeian1988significance, @meng1992comparing, @bond2004seeing] that could be used to put a standard error on the canonical subspace metric. I prefer the randomized prediction intervals for two reasons. First, the comparison to randomization provides a more intuitive way of understanding uncertainty in the word association problem than the distributional result. For example, the prediction intervals could be discretely interpolated toward the observed metric by randomizing only a subset of the words in either list; this could be used to ascertain the leave-one-out sensitivity of the comparison. Second, because the input metric is intrinsically multidimensional, our uncertainty about it is also hypervolumetric; treating our uncertainty about the canonical subspace metric as a scalar interval obscures this fact. Alternatively, researchers could take advantage of distributional results for eigenvalues from random matrix theory (e.g. CITE Johnstone 2001).


### Results

Table 1 compares the performance of the MCS and CCA metric-based models on the ten WEAT measures of semantic bias presented in the original paper. MCS-based WEAT measures tend to be inflated related to the canonical subspace metric. The MCS estimate for WEAT 8 is closest in magnitude but has the opposite sign. The median error in magnitude is approximately 4.2 times the corresponding canonical subspace metric, but magnitude errors in the other direction are possible. Additionally, the nested difference in means design of the test masks variation in the list-pairwise similarity metrics. MCS correctly estimates the order statistics for the four pairwise comparisons only for one test (WEAT 10).

Figure 1 demonstrates that the MCS estimator $\text{Sim}^*(I, J) := (1/k^2) \sum_{q=i} \sum_{q=j} \cos([W]^k_i, [W]^k_j)$ is not geometrically consistent for $q \geq 3, k \geq 4$. To show this, we must consider the lattice of all possible analyses involving subsets of words in a keyword list $A$. Each column of heatmaps depicts the lattice of canonical subspace metrics (left) mean cosine similarities (center panel) between every subset of the keyword list at the top of the figure. Each cell of the heatmap corresponds to the metric over the corresponding $q$-subset. A reasonable heuristic predictor of inconsistency is the 2-norm condition number of the cosine similarity matrix (see Fig. 1; right panel); the lower this value, the more likely it is that a subspace of dimension $q$ will be confused for one of its counterparts.

Figure 2 displays the canonical subspace metric (Fig. 2; left panel) and the corresponding MCS metric (Fig. 2; center panel) over the lattice of comparisons between subsets of the keyword lists. In the right panel, the full distribution of metrics corresponding to each heatmap is displayed; the dots indicate (in vertical order) the maximum value, expectation, and minimum value of the metric over $q$. In the right panel only, the mean of the *squared* cosine similarities is used to show the equivalence with the canonical subspace metric for the unidimensional problem. The expectation of the MCS metric over all possible sub-analyses of equivalent dimension is decreasing in the input dimension, while the expected canonical subspace metric increases monotonically in the number of dimensions as desired. As the number of cosine similarity estimates corresponding to the size of the analysis increases, the association between any pair of words already in the list remains fixed with respect to the new words. This causes MCS to converge to the expected coplanar angle in the input vector space as we increase $k$. In other words, MCS is a particular estimator of the expected cosine similarity between *any two vectors* in $X$ and $Y$, and it does not measure what or how much *all of the vectors* have in common.

Figure 3 displays the canonical congruences for the four subspace pairs compared to the three possible expected distributions of minimal common subspace alignment in $W(k)$. The corresponding WEAT score component for each metric is shown for comparison (MCS: dotted line; CCA: dashed line). Any comparison implies three reference distributions: the distribution obtained by randomizing both keyword lists, and the two distributions obtained by randomizing one list while holding the other fixed. There is no necessary relationship between these distributions, so there are many different answers to the question of whether an association is larger or smaller than what we would expect. One particularly interesting comparison is the difference between the estimate's relation to the two-way null and its relation to one or both of the one-way nulls. The association can be simultaneously smaller than what we would expect by a two-way random draw and larger than what we would expect by either one-way random draw, or vice-versa. There is no necessary relationship between the rank index of the estimated congruences and their positions with respect to their reference distributions; for example, only the eighth canonical congruence in the $\{\text{male, unpleasant}\}$ comparison is outside all three 95% prediction intervals.


## Discussion

WEAT-like measures are widely used in the social sciences to measure a wide range of cultural processes observable in text that traditionally were measured by human raters (CITE e.g [@kozlowski2019geometry; @nelson2021leveraging]). The key validity evidence for WEAT in this context is its agreement with human word association ratings (i.e., the IAT and similar psychological test-based methods). However, the convergent validity of the measure is weak evidence for its overall validity, particularly if it is not geometrically consistent. MCS does not satisfy this criterion. In practice, the canonical subspace metric is always a more consistent estimator of the targeted variation than MCS, and facilitates interpreting variation in the scale of observed associations in applied research. A general conclusion is that researchers should not use mean cosine similarity as a measure of multidimensional semantic association in applied statistical text analysis.

It is worth emphasizing that this result *cannot* be interpreted as evidence that stereotypes and biases do not exist. The canonical subspace metric surfaces word associations between gendered identity words and sentiment words with magnitude in excess of what we would expect from totally random selections of words. The more fundamental problem is that it is not clear why we should define (e.g.) stereotypical association for Black names with respect to white names, or biases against women with respect to men [@johfre2021reconsidering]. The results in this paper challenge the notion that there are unambiguously categorically opposed sets of words that would justify this analytic approach. In some contexts male/female and white/Black are talked about as if they are opposites, but this is only one limited perspective on the vast spectrum of similarities, differences, and ambiguities indexed by gender and racial identity [@butler1990gender; @hobbs2014chosen]. Reliance on keyword lists as a priori representations of "concepts" ("attributes", "identities", "schemas", etc.) renders this measurement approach dependent on the reader's intuitive acceptance of the concept label, rather than evidence that the keywords specifically pick out this concept. It is logically inconsistent to presume the meaning of words in advance of seeing their contexts if we are trying to learn word meanings by observing the contextual use of language [@wittgenstein1953pi].

Multidimensional similarity metrics within subspaces. Each column forms a lattice over the set of comparisons between subspaces. Each row increases the subspace dimensionality by one (top row is 1, bottom row is 7). Red dots indicate the row/column maximum (note the matrices are symmetric). A geometrically consistent similarity measure for multidimensional word association problems must locate all of the maxima on the diagonal. The canonical subspace metric satisfies this criterion; the mean cosine similarity metric does not (heatmaps, left panel). Geometric inconsistency is partially predictable from the hyperelliptical elongation (condition number) of the $k$-simplex described by each cosine similarity matrix (scatterplots, right panel).

#### Figure 2.
Multidimensional similarity metrics between subspaces. Cell colors indicate more commonality between subsets (heatmaps, left panel). The solid red (canonical subspace) and blue (mean squared cosine similarity) lines indicate their respective expectations. The dashed lines indicate the maximum and minimum values at each dimensionality. The canonical subspace metric increases as we gain more information about the common semantics of the input word. When the word association problem involves only one-to-one word pairings, the canonical subspace metric is equivalent to the *squared* cosine similarity. The mean cosine similarity decreases toward the global mean as more words are added to the analysis, whereas the canonical subspace metric increases.

#### Figure 3.
Canonical congruences (red diamonds) with 95% prediction intervals for the one- and two-way null distributions. Blue intervals correspond to the one-way null distributions holding the pleasant/unpleasant lists constant while randomizing the male/female lists. Yellow intervals correspond to the one-way null distributions holding the male/female lists constant while randomizing the pleasant/unpleasant lists. Green intervals randomize both lists. The mean cosine similarity metric for each comparison is plotted as the pink dotted line; the canonical subspace metric is plotted as the red dashed line.
